projects.summary: Frontend: the customer-facing shop, cart and checkout.
projects.story:
The online shop customers actually see: product listings, filters, the cart and a three-step checkout. Pages are server-rendered, with a thin layer of TypeScript for the interactive parts.

Conversion dipped after the last redesign. Support is fielding tickets about prices, promo codes and a search box that feels sluggish, and an accessibility audit came back with a long list.

## What you'll work on

- Formatting money and other values the way customers expect to read them
- Form behaviour, validation and accessible markup
- Small performance fixes in the browser, like debouncing input

## Good fit if you

- Build user interfaces, or want to get sharper at the details that make one feel solid
- Are comfortable with **JavaScript**, **TypeScript** or plain **HTML**
- Care what a bug looks like from the customer's side of the screen

Stack: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML.

The service every client talks to for sign-up, login, sessions and password resets. Most of it is Go, a few older endpoints are still PHP, the admin back office is a small Ruby app, the password service is Java, and the login gateway in front is TypeScript.

## What you'll work on

- Parsing and validating request parameters with sensible defaults
- Time and expiry logic, where off-by-one and unit mix-ups hide
- Rate limiting and log handling for the people on call

## Good fit if you

- Like **input validation**, edge cases and reading a stack trace at 2am
- Know **Go**, **PHP**, **Ruby**, **Java** or **TypeScript**, or want to try one of them on familiar problems

Stack: Go, PHP, Ruby, Java, TypeScript.

src/isExpired.php.text:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

/**
 * Whether a password reset link has expired. Timestamps are Unix seconds;
 * a link stays valid until $issuedAt + $ttlMinutes * 60, inclusive.
 */
function isExpired(int $issuedAt, int $now, int $ttlMinutes): bool
{
    return $now > $issuedAt + $ttlMinutes;
}

tests/IsExpiredTest.php.text:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

use PHPUnit\Framework\Attributes\DataProvider;
use PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase;

// Acceptance criteria for API-2. The checks run against these cases.
final class IsExpiredTest extends TestCase
{
    /** [arguments, expected] as JSON. */
    public static function cases(): array
    {
        return [
            'case 1' => ['[1000,1059,60]', 'false'],
            'case 2' => ['[1000,4600,60]', 'false'],
            'case 3' => ['[1000,4601,60]', 'true'],
            'case 4' => ['[1000,1000,0]', 'false'],
        ];
    }

    #[DataProvider('cases')]
    public function testIsExpired(string $input, string $expected): void
    {
        $args = json_decode($input, true);
        $actual = isExpired(...$args);
        $this->assertSame(json_decode($expected, true), $actual);
    }
}

sha256:43c9f82af02d2540c0391d7937fbd6f2c.body: `slugify(name)` turns a workspace name into its URL slug: lowercase ASCII letters and digits, with every run of anything else between words becoming a single hyphen, and no hyphen at either end. Accented Latin letters lose their accents first, so `"Café Ünïcorn"` becomes `"cafe-unicorn"`.

lib/slugify.rb.text:
# Workspace URLs are /w/<slug>. Turn a workspace name into its slug:
# lowercase ASCII letters and digits, words joined by single hyphens.
def slugify(name)
  name.downcase.tr(" ", "-")
end

# Shop

The online shop customers actually see: product listings, filters, the cart and a three-step checkout. Pages are server-rendered, with a thin layer of TypeScript for the interactive parts.

Conversion dipped after the last redesign. Support is fielding tickets about prices, promo codes and a search box that feels sluggish, and an accessibility audit came back with a long list.

## What you'll work on

- Formatting money and other values the way customers expect to read them
- Form behaviour, validation and accessible markup
- Small performance fixes in the browser, like debouncing input

## Good fit if you

- Build user interfaces, or want to get sharper at the details that make one feel solid
- Are comfortable with **JavaScript**, **TypeScript** or plain **HTML**
- Care what a bug looks like from the customer's side of the screen

Stack: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML.

templates/filter-form-labels.html.text:
<!--
  Product filters on the category page. The accessibility audit flagged these
  checkboxes: each needs a label tied to it.
-->
<form>
  <input type="checkbox" name="in-stock"> in-stock
  <input type="checkbox" name="on-sale"> on-sale
</form>

text: The accessibility audit flagged every checkbox here. Clicking the text should toggle the box.

sha256:dce849a205d06e1a4764c66140bd06b80.body: `ParsePage(query)` reads `page` and `per_page` from a URL query string. Defaults are page 1 and 20 per page, `per_page` is capped at 100, and missing, zero, negative or non-numeric values fall back to the default.

README.md.text:
# Accounts API

The service every client talks to for sign-up, login, sessions and password resets. Most of it is Go, a few older endpoints are still PHP, the admin back office is a small Ruby app, the password service is Java, and the login gateway in front is TypeScript.

It mostly works, and the on-call channel has opinions about the rest: list endpoints that accept any page size, reset links that expire too soon, and logs that are hard to search during an incident.

## What you'll work on

- Parsing and validating request parameters with sensible defaults
- Time and expiry logic, where off-by-one and unit mix-ups hide
- Rate limiting and log handling for the people on call

## Good fit if you

- Write backend services, or want practice with the bugs they actually get
- Like **input validation**, edge cases and reading a stack trace at 2am
- Know **Go**, **PHP**, **Ruby**, **Java** or **TypeScript**, or want to try one of them on familiar problems

Stack: Go, PHP, Ruby, Java, TypeScript.

text: The mobile app sends per_page=500 to fetch everything in one go. Cap it, don't error.

sha256:ddd685e7390e621bf103680a2dffee5f5.body: Simulate an LRU cache with the given capacity over operations `["put", key, value]` and `["get", key]`. Return the results of the gets in order, `-1` for a miss. A get counts as a use.

README.md.text:
# Edge proxy

A small proxy in front of everything: it terminates connections, caches hot responses and exports latency metrics. The hot path is C and C++; the control plane and metrics are Go.

Every allocation shows up on a flame graph here. The backlog is about doing more with fixed memory, measuring the right thing, and keeping configuration readable for whoever is paged.

## What you'll work on

- Fixed-size data structures such as ring buffers and LRU caches
- Latency percentiles and the metrics behind dashboards
- Small, strict configuration formats

## Good fit if you

- Do systems or performance work, or want to get closer to the metal
- Think about memory, ordering and what happens under load
- Know **C**, **C++** or **Go**, or are learning one of them

Stack: C, C++, Go.

text: Hit rate dropped to 12% after the last deploy. I think get() stopped refreshing recency.

hints.text: Pair a hash map with a doubly linked list ordered by last use.

sha256:e29497404701da3bc698b3b6f4e4e5565.body: Given `orders(id, customer)` and `payments(order_id, amount)`, select the ids of orders that have no payment, smallest first.

queries/unpaid-orders.sql.text:
-- Month-end close: orders that have no matching payment, smallest id first.
-- orders(id, customer), payments(order_id, amount)
SELECT id
FROM orders;

README.md.text:
# Data platform

Partners drop CSV exports in a bucket every night. A pipeline cleans them, loads the warehouse and feeds the reports finance reads on Monday morning.

The exports are messier than anyone admits: quoted commas in company names, duplicate customers with slightly different emails, and orders that never got paid. When the numbers look wrong, this is where people come asking.

## What you'll work on

- Parsing awkward input files without losing data
- Cleaning and deduplicating records before they reach the warehouse
- SQL for the reports and reconciliations people rely on

## Good fit if you

- Work with data, or are the person on your team who ends up writing the SQL
- Enjoy turning messy input into something you can trust
- Know **Python**, **SQL** or **C#**, or want more practice with them

Stack: Python, SQL, and C# for the billing jobs.

text: Month-end close is Friday. I need this list before then.

hints.text: A LEFT JOIN keeps orders even when no payment matches.

sha256:e359a096b7c0455ff5dd4e21cf035bd1d.body: `Percentile(samples, p)` returns the nearest-rank percentile: sort the samples and take the value at rank `ceil(p / 100 × n)`, counting from 1. With no samples, `ok` is false (shown as `null` in the checks).
